'''Marissa Kawehi Loving''' is an American [[Pure mathematics|theoretical mathematician]]. In 2022, she joined the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin-Madison]] as the Assistant Professor of Mathematics. Loving, who is both [[Native Hawaiians|native Hawaiʻian]] and [[Black people|Black]], was the first woman faculty member from a historically excluded racial group in mathematics to receive [[Academic tenure|tenure-track]] in the department.<ref name=":1" /> She was recognised as one of the 2023 Black Mathematician Honorees by [[Mathematically Gifted & Black|Mathematically Gifted and Black]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Marissa Kawehi Loving |url=https://mathematicallygiftedandblack.com/honorees/marissa-kawehi-loving/ |access-date=2026-08-15 |language=en-US |url-status=live |archive-date=2026-08-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260815125603/https://mathematicallygiftedandblack.com/honorees/marissa-kawehi-loving/ |website=mathematicallygiftedandblack.com}}</ref>

Loving's research interests include [[geometric group theory]], [[low-dimensional topology]] and mapping [[Class of groups|class groups]] of finite and infinite surfaces.<ref name=":1" />

== Early life and education ==
Loving was born in [[Oʻahu|O'ahu]], [[Hawaiʻi (island)|Hawaiʻi]] and raised in [[Honomū, Hawaii|Honomū]].<ref name=":2" /> In addition to being a [[Native Hawaiians|Native Hawaiʻian]], she is also Black, Puerto Rican, and Japanese.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=History of Women Mathematicians |url=https://www.math.wisc.edu/history-of-women-mathematicians/ |access-date=2026-08-15 |website=Department of Mathematics |language=en-US |archive-date=2026-08-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260815115745/https://www.math.wisc.edu/history-of-women-mathematicians/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Her mother Theresa Loving (née Prowell) was from [[Pennsylvania]] and her father, Floyd Carleton Loving lll, was a middle-school mathematics teacher from O'ahu. Loving is the eldest of 11 siblings.<ref name=":3" /> She was homeschooled, and was more interested in pursuing writing, instead of STEM, as a career.<ref name=":2" /> She wanted to be a journalist or a playwright, but decided to study computer science at the [[University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo|University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo]], where she was a presidential scholar.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=LovingMath |url=https://sites.google.com/view/lovingmath/home |access-date=2026-08-15 |website=sites.google.com |language=en-US |archive-date=2026-03-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260308050511/https://sites.google.com/view/lovingmath/home |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Mānoa: Spring commencement ceremony to be held on Saturday, May 11 |url=https://manoa.hawaii.edu/news/article.php?aId=5744 |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=University of Hawaii News}}</ref>

Loving graduated from the University of Hawaiʻi in 2013 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in computer science and a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in mathematics.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2024-04-09 |title=Dr. Marissa Kawehi Loving |url=https://www.gwisbeta.org/dr-marissa-kawehi-loving/ |access-date=2026-08-15 |website=Graduate Women In Science |language=en-US |archive-date=2025-10-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251004082756/https://www.gwisbeta.org/dr-marissa-kawehi-loving/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":1" /> She earned a doctorate degree in mathematics from [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] in 2019, during which she received the [[NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program|NSF Graduate Research Fellowship]] and an Illinois Graduate College Distinguished Fellowship.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> 
She was the first Native Hawaiian woman to earn a PhD in mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://events.brown.edu/mathematics/event/215080-horizons-seminar-marissa-kawehi-loving|title=Horizons Seminar: Marissa Kawehi Loving|first=Brown Office of University|last=Communications|website=events.brown.edu}}</ref> For the next three years, she was NSF Postdoctoral Research Fellow and Hale Assistant Professor at [[Georgia Tech]]. In 2022, she joined [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin-Madison]] as an Assistant Professor on a tenure-track position and earned the [[Nellie Y. McKay]] Fellowship.<ref name=":0" /> Loving is the first woman from a historically excluded racial group in mathematics to be appointed as a tenure-track faculty member in the department.<ref name=":1" />

== Research ==
Loving' contributions in the field of low-dimensional topology focus on end-periodic mapping tori ({{Singular}} [[torus]]) to understand the [[hyperbolic volume]]s and [[Geometric invariant theory|geometric invariants]] that inform broader [[manifold]] classification. In particular, she links surface dynamics to 3-dimensional hyperbolic geometry by establishing the bounds on volumes for the tori. Building on the work of [[Ian Agol]] and [[Jeffrey Brock]] on hyperbolic [[3-manifold]]s in the finite-type setting, Loving worked with Elizabeth Field, Heejoung Kim, and Chris Leininger to construct and subsequently use "a broad class of examples of irreducible, end-periodic [[homeomorphism]]s" to show an [[Asymptote|asymptotic]]ally sharp bound.<ref>{{Cite web |title=End periodic homeomorphisms and volumes of mapping tori |url=https://math.duke.edu/events/end-periodic-homeomorphisms-and-volumes-mapping-tori |access-date=2026-08-23 |website=Department of Mathematics |archive-date=2026-08-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260824194657/https://math.duke.edu/events/end-periodic-homeomorphisms-and-volumes-mapping-tori |url-status=live |publisher=[[Duke University]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Field |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Kim |first2=Heejoung |last3=Leininger |first3=Christopher |last4=Loving |first4=Marissa |date=2023 |title=End-periodic homeomorphisms and volumes of mapping tori |url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1112/topo.12277 |journal=Journal of Topology |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=57–105 |doi=10.1112/topo.12277 |issn=1753-8416}}</ref> She, alongside Field, [[Autumn Kent]], and Leininger, devised "a framework to prove volume estimates for closed hyperbolic 3-manifolds with depth-one [[foliation]]s."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Field |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Kent |first2=Autumn |last3=Leininger |first3=Christopher |last4=Loving |first4=Marissa |date=2025 |title=A lower bound on volumes of end-periodic mapping tori |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/topo.70037 |journal=Journal of Topology |language=en |volume=18 |issue=3 |article-number=e70037 |doi=10.1112/topo.70037 |issn=1753-8424}}</ref>

Loving's work also involves big mapping [[Class of groups|class groups]], in particular those arising from infinite-type surfaces. Using [[geometric group theory]] techniques, she and Justin Lanier demonstrated that subgroup structures of infinite-type surfaces have trivial centers and that every non-trivial [[normal subgroup]] contains a [[Non-abelian group|non-abelian free group]].<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Lanier |first1=Justin |title=Centers of subgroups of big mapping class groups and the Tits alternative |date=2019-04-22 |eprint=1904.10060 |last2=Loving |first2=Marissa |class=math.GT }}</ref>

== Other engagements ==
In 2019, Loving and fellow mathematician Justin Lanier founded SUBgroups, a network of online support groups, to help first-year math graduate students to connect with their peers in order to share their experiences, uplift each other, and find a mathematical community beyond their academic program.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-03-30 |title=Postdoc Marissa Loving is the Subject of Award Winning Essay |url=https://math.gatech.edu/news/postdoc-marissa-loving-subject-award-winning-essay |access-date=2026-08-17 |website=School of Mathematics {{!}} Georgia Institute of Technology {{!}} Atlanta, GA |language=en |archive-date=2026-03-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260305080921/https://math.gatech.edu/news/postdoc-marissa-loving-subject-award-winning-essay |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-08-20 |title=How it works |url=https://gradsubgroups.org/how-it-works/ |access-date=2026-08-17 |website=SUBgroups |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/202101/rnoti-p63.pdf|title=Building equity-minded online programs|access-date=2026-08-27|archive-date=2025-05-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250506053242/https://www.ams.org/notices/202101/rnoti-p63.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> She also cofounded paraDIGMS (Diversity in Graduate Mathematical Sciences) to provide resources, support, and collaboration opportunities to a professional community of graduate directors, graduate committee members, department chairs, and faculty. She coordinates the activities for paraDIGMS alongside Lanier, Matthew Ando (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) and [[Bianca Viray]] ([[University of Washington]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=paraDIGMS: Diversity in Graduate Mathematical Sciences |url=https://www.ams.org/learning-careers/leaders/paraDIGMS |access-date=2026-08-17 |website=[[American Mathematical Society]]}}</ref><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Marissa Kawehi Loving |url=https://indigenousmathematicians.org/marissa-kawehi-loving/ |access-date=2026-08-17 |website=Indigenous Mathematicians |language=en-US |archive-date=2025-10-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251004082545/https://indigenousmathematicians.org/marissa-kawehi-loving/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Loving serves on the [[Pacific Institute for the Mathematical Sciences]]' Indigenous Engagement Committee, which supports Indigenous-led efforts in education and research in the mathematical sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marissa Loving |url=https://pims.math.ca/profiles/marissa-loving |access-date=2026-08-23 |website=Pacific Institute for the Mathematical Sciences |archive-date=2026-08-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260824115731/https://pims.math.ca/profiles/marissa-loving |url-status=live }}</ref> She is the cofounder of Indigenous Mathematicians, a web platform that recognizes indigenous people in mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Crowell |first=Rachel |title=Modern Mathematics Confronts Its White, Patriarchal Past |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/modern-mathematics-confronts-its-white-patriarchal-past/ |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=About Us |url=https://indigenousmathematicians.org/about-us/ |access-date=2026-08-27 |website=Indigenous Mathematicians |language=en-US}}</ref>
